title: Washout seals top spot for Nepal. Sri Lanka wait in quarterfinals - The Kathmandu Post
description: Washout seals top spot for Nepal. Sri Lanka wait in quarterfinals  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s final preliminary group match of the 20th Asian Games against hosts Japan was abandoned due to heavy rain on Saturday, but the Rhinos had already done enough to advance as Group A’s topper and book a quarterfinal clash against Sri Lanka .

Put into bat after losing the toss at Korogi Athletic Park in Aichi, Nepal managed 149/4 in a match shortened by rain to 15 overs per side.

However, persistent torrential downpours following the conclusion of Nepal’s innings forced the umpires to call off the fixture. Nepal and Japan then shared points.

Having defeated Afghanistan by five wickets on Friday, Nepal topped Group A to seal their spot in the last eight. Hosts Japan, who had lost to Afghanistan, were eliminated from the competition.

In the quarterfinal stage, group winners Nepal will face seeded heavyweights Sri Lanka for a place in the semifinals. Group A runners-up Afghanistan will take on India in another quarterfinal fixture.

Rain also disrupted Group B action on Saturday, with the second match between Malaysia and Oman abandoned without a single ball being bowled. Group B winners Malaysia advance to face Bangladesh in the quarterfinals, while runners-up Hong Kong take on Pakistan.

Earlier in the day, explosive half-centuries from Sundeep Jora and Lokesh Bam set up Nepal’s formidable total. Jora remained undefeated on a belligerent 57 off 32 balls, while Bam stayed not out at 52 off 22 deliveries. The pair combined for a 65-run partnership off 30 balls for the fifth wicket.

After openers Kushal Bhurtel (4 off 12) and Aasif Sheikh (21 off 15) fell cheaply alongside Kushal Malla (2 off 5) and Gulshan Jha (2 off 6), Jora took charge of the innings with supreme confidence, hammering five fours and three sixes. He reached his half-century when a Japanese fielder dropped a catch at the boundary ropes on 49, resulting in a boundary.

At the other end, Bam, who also got a lifeline, brought up his maiden T20I half-century in thrilling fashion, launching a six off the final ball of the innings. Striking one four and six sixes, Bam brought the crowd of nearly 2,000 Nepali supporters to their feet.

For Japan, Reo Sakurano-Thomas, Ibrahim Takahashi, Jake Kusuda-Nairn and Declan Suzuki picked up a wicket each.

title: Rescued worker ready to help rebuild Nepal - Taipei Times
description: Rescued worker ready to help rebuild Nepal  Taipei Times
publisher.title: Taipei Times
full_article:
Rescued worker ready to help rebuild Nepal

BY ANUP Ojha / AFP, KIRTIPUR, Nepal

Add TT as Preferred Source



Rescued alive 10 days after catastrophic floods trapped him in a tunnel, Nepalese hydropower worker Kabir Maharjan is determined to help rebuild his country despite his own harrowing ordeal.

Traditional music and tearful relatives welcomed the 45-year-old when he returned home on Friday after spending weeks recovering at a hospital in Kathmandu.

“Life is precious. Hundreds of people have died but I survived,” the father of two said in an interview, his voice choked with emotion. “Perhaps I still have work to do for my society, for the country, and my home and family.”

Soldiers disembark a helicopter carrying Kabir Maharjan, a worker who was trapped inside a tunnel of the Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, as they arrive at Chhauni Army Hospital in Kathmandu on Sept. 4 Photo: AFP

The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse near the China-Nepal border, killed at least 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.

More than 5,000 people remain missing in Nepal after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous northern regions, and battered crucial hydropower projects.

displayDFP('ad-IR1', 'm');

Maharjan, who was among hundreds of workers employed at projects hit by the floods, was eventually airlifted from the worst-hit Rasuwa region.

His miraculous rescue on Sept. 4, alongside fellow worker Sanjay Sah, offered a rare moment of hope during the disaster.

As Nepal shifts from emergency response to reconstruction, he said he hopes to return to his profession.

“There is risk in everything, but still we have to win over it,” he said.

In Nepal, more than 800 hydropower project workers remain unaccounted for, the energy minister told parliament last week.

Rescue teams continue to comb through the ruins, and 47 bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites.

Maharjan said he survived by reaching an upper floor of the tunnel site and drinking water while waiting for help.

“Whenever I was awake, I would try to find a way out,” he said. Days later, he saw what appeared to be a light and heard voices. “I thought I imagined it. But I called out, and they answered.”

For Maharjan, the country’s long road to recovery mirrors his own — he is still recovering from wounds on his hand and leg.

He said the rebuilding efforts could provide spiritual sustenance.

“While we are alive we must be patient and do our work,” he said. “Work is our karma.”

The flooding dealt a major blow to Nepal’s hydropower generation system, which is central to the country’s development ambitions and export earnings.

The government estimates overall reconstruction could cost US$4.8 billion, with thousands of people displaced and key infrastructure damaged.

The disaster has renewed scrutiny of how roads, hydropower plants and trade corridors are built in Nepal’s challenging mountain terrain.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN on Thursday that the flooding was “a warning to the world” about the growing dangers posed by climate change, urging greater international support to help Nepal adapt and rebuild.

Aid groups have warned that the humanitarian crisis is far from over.

“The floodwaters may have receded, but for thousands of people, the crisis is far from over,” David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal, said on Friday. “It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty.”

title: Expert blames climate change for Nepal flash floods | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News - nhk.or.jp
description: Expert blames climate change for Nepal flash floods | NHK WORLD-JAPAN News  nhk.or.jp
publisher.title: nhk.or.jp
full_article:
A Nepalese expert on glaciers says climate change played a significant role in the massive flash floods that devastated border areas between Nepal and China.

Sudan Bikash Maharjan is a researcher at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, based in Kathmandu. He spoke to NHK on Thursday about his analysis of topographical data and satellite images to identify the cause of the flash floods.

Maharjan said the studies suggest the possibility that a glacier at an altitude of about 5,100 meters had melted, exposing part of the rock surface of the slope, and that melted water had permeated into the rock through cracks, making the slope unstable.

He said the analysis shows when the glacier and huge rock mass collapsed, the debris fell about 1,000 meters and crashed into another glacier at the bottom of the valley. He said the frictional energy and force of the collision melted and pulverized the valley glacier, resulting in water and debris gushing down the valley.

Maharjan said climate change played a significant role in the occurrence of the deadly flooding. He pointed out that the glacier area across Nepal has decreased by 32 percent just over a 40-year period. He said climate change, especially rising temperatures, has caused a substantial loss in glacier area by accelerating the pace of melting.

He also warned that changes in the landscape of the valley due to the disaster could significantly increase the risk of landslides and flooding in the future.

He said systems to issue alarms and monitor conditions in the mountain regions should be strengthened to prepare for future calamities.

title: B.C. family still looking for answers 1 month after deadly Nepal flood - CBC
description: B.C. family still looking for answers 1 month after deadly Nepal flood  CBC
publisher.title: CBC
full_article:
One month after a deadly flooding event in Nepal, a B.C. family is among several Canadians still waiting for answers.

Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered and over 5,600 people remain missing — the Canadian Press reports — a month after a catastrophic flash flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet on Aug. 26.

Global Affairs Canada said on Saturday that 29 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing.

Coquitlam, B.C., couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among them, according to family.

"We are still clueless," said Shubakshi’s cousin Vikram Khosla.

The couple lived with their two daughters — one a teenager and one in her early 20s, he said.

"We are helpless, we can’t do anything," said Khosla.

2 trapped workers rescued from hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods

He said the couple and their two daughters had been in India visiting family at the time, when Sumit and Shubakshi took a trip to the Himalayas for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

The couple spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck, but nobody has heard from them since then, said Khosla.

He said the daughters are back in Canada and various family members are taking turns caring for them.

WATCH | Why the Nepal flood was almost impossible to predict: Why you can’t predict a disaster like Nepal’s flood | About That September 3 | Duration 2:58 A collapsed glacier in Nepal caused catastrophic flooding that killed more than a thousand people, while thousands more are still missing. Andrew Chang breaks down what accelerated the flood to such a violent degree and how factors like the scale of the Himalayan mountains and the region's climate make prediction and monitoring so challenging. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

The federal government says Canadian officials continue to work with authorities in Nepal and China to support efforts to locate the missing Canadians and provide assistance to affected families.

"Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be provided, and we cannot comment on what is being discussed with families," said the statement.

Global Affairs Canada would not specify how many of the missing Canadians are from B.C., but CBC News has spoken with the family of another missing couple from Port Moody — Dhaval and Megha Shah .

Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla, pictured with loved ones, are among 29 Canadians still missing since the flash flood, according to family members. (Submitted by Vikram Khosla)

Despite no news on his cousin, Khosla says the family holds onto hope that they can be found.

"Everyone keeps praying every single day, hoping that maybe they are injured, maybe they are somewhere stuck and maybe we will get to hear something about them," he said.

Khosla described the couple as "beautiful souls." He said the couple took care of others and were part of a very happy family.

"It’s hard to believe that something like that happened to them," he said. "I don’t know why they had to be there at that time."

title: U.S. Says It Seeks to Expand Economic Ties With Nepal, Not Force Geopolitical Choices - nepyork
description: U.S. Says It Seeks to Expand Economic Ties With Nepal, Not Force Geopolitical Choices  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — The United States does not intend to ask Nepal to choose between Washington, Beijing and New Delhi. Instead, it wants to offer Kathmandu economic and commercial alternatives, a senior State Department official told NepYork.

“Similar to Bangladesh, where I don’t think we’re going to any country — and you’ll hear the Secretary talk about this — and say you have to choose,” the official said when asked how the United States views Nepal’s sovereignty as the Himalayan nation balances its relations with India and China.

“But what we want to do is we want to provide alternatives,” the official said. “We want to provide — for Nepal in particular, we’ve been very interested in increasing our commercial engagement.”

The official said the United States sees investment and business ties as a key area for strengthening the bilateral relationship.

“So for the first time ever this year, Nepal — I think they amended their law last year about outbound investment,” the official said. “We had the first Nepali delegation come to SelectUSA, the event that the Department of Commerce hosts.”

Asked about Nepal’s efforts to balance its relations with its two larger neighbors, the official acknowledged the country’s difficult geopolitical position.

“And so when we talk about balancing, we understand Nepal — I mean, you look at the map,” the official said. “They’re in a very — they’re in a tough spot in the world.”

The official said Nepal maintains a strong relationship with India and that Washington wants Nepal to have greater opportunities to deepen ties with the United States and other Western countries.

“They have a good relationship with India, and we want — we want to be able to provide that opportunity for them to also look to the West and have better relations with us,” the official said. “And that’s what we’re building towards.”

title: A change of consciousness: Nepal’s new political moment - Khabarhub
description: A change of consciousness: Nepal’s new political moment  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
It may not be a fascinating proposition, but getting politics right is the most important task. Without it, pioneering efforts to build modern political institutions, embrace pluralism, strengthen constitutional government, and develop a thriving economy cannot be sustained. The consolidation of modern politics and the emergence of democratic forces pressing for change can foster a desire for good governance and make broader progress possible.

Above all, protecting individual rights and creating an environment capable of overcoming new forms of social and political division can help contain violence and establish the conditions for genuine political progress. This is the point Stephen Marche (2022) emphasizes.

Here again, political nihilism may seem increasingly old-fashioned, even backward, as decentralized forms of political organization and governance gain ground. Yet the rise of the corporate state carries profound political consequences. It can concentrate power in ways that leave citizens with diminishing control over the forces shaping their lives.

More fundamentally, the emergence of the corporate state can produce a profit-driven political system whose driving force is the concentration, expansion, and preservation of state power and control, with potentially grave consequences.

Some people may understandably feel uncomfortable with this political transformation and respond with resentment, suspicion, or negativity.

The road ahead is grim. Mass political culture tells us that despite material progress and prosperity, a spirit of unhappiness and depression increasingly haunts market democracies around the world. This challenges the idea that markets necessarily maximize human well-being, as well as the eighteenth-century promise of the right to pursue happiness under governments chosen by the people themselves.

While Nepal cannot fully escape the gravitational pull of neoliberalism, it is equally clear that the country will not be redeemed by a solitary, independent-minded figure who rises above party labels and dissolves partisan boundaries. Such a unifying presence is not waiting in the wings.

What remains uncertain is whether the RSP government can cultivate the deeper political maturity needed to move beyond the kakistocratic habits that, in my view, have shaped Nepal’s governance since 2008. The question is not merely institutional but existential: Can a political culture accustomed to decay learn to imagine itself anew?

Nepal today increasingly resembles two estranged Nepali publics—communities that distrust, resent, and even despise one another. The political middle ground, once a space for negotiation and shared purpose, has all but vanished. In this fractured landscape, the RSP itself risks appearing less like a reformist force and more like a consortium of plutocrats. Vasily Grossman, the Russian novelist, as quoted by Chris Hedges in Empire of Illusion (2008), reminds us that the struggle between good and evil is never abstract; it is lived daily in the choices societies make. His warning—that evil triumphs when people fail to resist it—feels acutely relevant to Nepal’s present moment.

The deeper challenge, then, is to move beyond anger, retaliation, and the short-term calculations that dominate political life. Nepal must cultivate a practical wisdom capable of strengthening collective dignity, social cohesion, and the quality of everyday life. Such transformation is slow, often imperceptible, but without it, neither political change nor economic progress can produce a society that feels stable, hopeful, or whole. Renewal requires not only new policies but a new sensibility—a shift in how citizens and leaders understand their shared fate.

Comparative political research reminds us that institutions unable to adapt to shifting realities often drift toward stagnation and lose the moral authority that sustains them. The RSP government’s challenge, therefore, is not simply administrative; it must demonstrate change that is felt, seen, and trusted. Only then can this political transition become a genuine renewal rather than another repetition of familiar disappointments. The deeper test is whether Nepal’s institutions can rediscover the vitality that once animated democratic aspiration.

Scholars increasingly observe that what once seemed unimaginable has begun to seep into everyday life. No society, however stable it appears, is immune to internal fractures. The descent from relative prosperity into unrest rarely follows a single thread; it emerges from a dense weave of insecurity, polarization, distrust, corruption, and the slow erosion of faith in public institutions.

These pressures accumulate quietly until a society finds itself struggling to restore coherence. In his book The Next Civil War , Stephen Marche describes the possibility of the United States—the world’s most enduring democracy and largest economy—descending into a profound internal crisis. The prospect is deeply unsettling, for the consequences would be devastating.

Conceptually, alternatives always exist; human societies are never locked into a single path. Yet when hatred saturates public discourse, when discouragement replaces hope, when corporate scandals become routine, and when governments appear beholden to powerful interests, democratic institutions begin to lose their moral grounding. In such an atmosphere, opposition becomes reactive rather than constructive, and political actors respond to fear rather than wisdom. The erosion is subtle but profound: a society forgets how to imagine a future beyond its grievances.

The March 2026 parliamentary elections marked a profound rupture with Nepal’s so-called established political forces. The RSP won 182 of the 275 seats, while the Nepali Congress won 38 and the UML 25. The result represented not merely a change in political fortunes but a powerful rejection of an established political elite whose long record had become associated, in the public imagination, with corruption, patronage, political privilege, and failure of governance.

For decades, politics too often became a mechanism for accumulating money, power, and personal privilege rather than advancing the common good. The result was an erosion of democratic culture and public trust. The country paid the price while political actors and their networks benefited from the system. Nepal cannot rebuild a healthier political order using the same assumptions, habits, and incentives that produced the old one. The familiar slogans, self-delusions, and self-serving political packages designed to manipulate the masses have lost much of their credibility, as demonstrated by the ballot box.

In particular, the long dominance of figures such as Oli, Dahal, Deuba, Bhattarai, and Madhab has left a political legacy that deserves rigorous scrutiny. Their periods in power were accompanied by persistent concerns over corruption, institutional weakness, political patronage, and the deterioration of public services. Political spectacle and partisan confrontation increasingly displaced constructive democratic discourse, while powerful interests were often perceived as receiving preferential treatment over broader public interests.

Yet elections exposed the limits of this political formula. The old slogans and political narratives could no longer conceal the accumulated grievances of citizens. The electorate produced a dramatic change in the composition of Parliament and opened space for a new political generation.

For the first time in decades, the NC and UML have found themselves confronted with the consequences of their long-consolidated party rule and personality-driven leadership. Rather than attempting to preserve the old political order, they should allow space for a new political elite to emerge and do what is necessary and appropriate for Nepal and its people.

For the RSP government, however, the challenge extends beyond political transformation. It must also lead Nepal’s reconstruction following the devastating flash floods—an enormous and perhaps almost incalculable task.

Some people may understandably feel uncomfortable with this political transformation and respond with resentment, suspicion, or negativity. That is part of democratic life. Some politicians, civil society actors, media figures, and analysts have questioned aspects of the political transition or advanced competing interpretations of the events surrounding it. Such disagreement is legitimate in a democracy. The important question is whether these competing perspectives can develop sufficient public support to shape the country’s political direction.

That, too, is democracy.

Nepal has paid enough for political failure. The question now is simple but profound: Do we break the cycle, or repeat it?

Nepal’s democratic institutions still struggle to regulate market forces while protecting social equality and public welfare. Political elites continue to coexist with a crude form of capitalism that can privilege market interests under different forms of governance. If this remains unchanged, economic and social inequality could deepen in ways that are difficult to reconcile with a democracy founded on equal rights, opportunities, and duties.

The September 2025 Gen Z uprising and the March 2026 elections should be understood as intertwined expressions of a deeper transformation. The protests revealed a generation unwilling to accept corruption, inequality, and political stagnation as inevitable. The election that followed translated this dissatisfaction into a dramatic reshaping of Parliament.

Together, these events opened a path for Nepal to imagine a political order not bound by the habits of previous decades. This emerging consciousness echoes Einstein’s insight: problems cannot be solved from the same level of awareness that created them. Nepal now stands at a threshold where a shift in political sensibility may matter as much as institutional reform.

The challenge now is to understand how Nepal can move toward a democratic political order in which institutions rise above partisan struggle and restore legitimacy to a system weakened by years of decay. At a moment of profound turbulence and institutional challenge, there is no immediate formula for safeguarding the national interest.

The real test, therefore, is whether the RSP can rise above the political consciousness that brought down the old order—and build something fundamentally different: a democratic system that protects citizens, serves the public interest, strengthens institutions, and advances the national interest. Nepal has already paid a heavy price for political failure. What matters now is whether this new chapter can prevent the country from slipping back into the same cycle of disappointment, instability, and lost opportunity.

It is too early to forecast Nepal’s political future. But if the RSP fails to bring substantial change in governance, another youth uprising like the September 2025 Gen Z protests is likely.

For the RSP government, however, the challenge extends beyond political transformation. It must also lead Nepal’s reconstruction following the devastating flash floods—an enormous and perhaps almost incalculable task. The government must rebuild damaged infrastructure while preparing Nepal for an unpredictable future. Its real test, therefore, will not simply be whether it can govern, but whether it can transform this crisis into an opportunity to rebuild the country with greater resilience, institutional competence, and strategic foresight.

Indeed, the recent Bhotekoshi flash floods—an event that claimed thousands of lives and swept away entire settlements—confront us with a rare and devastating reminder of a truth most of us seldom witness: that suffering is woven into the human condition, often without warning or explanation. Catastrophes like this seem to undergo a kind of mysterious metamorphosis; they begin as natural events but quickly reveal the fragile architecture of our political and moral worlds. We know such disasters cannot always be prevented, yet survival—both physical and institutional—often hinges on the choices and conduct of those in power.

In this moment, I find myself unexpectedly moved by the Balen government’s response. Their actions do not erase the tragedy, but they gesture toward a form of governance that acknowledges vulnerability without surrendering to despair. It is a small but meaningful source of hope.

Disasters of this scale may never be fully predictable, but that does not mean we should retreat into willful ignorance or live under perpetual anxiety. Nepal must learn to inhabit a world where danger is a constant companion, not an aberration. Real life rarely unfolds along a neat, linear trajectory; more often, the path to survival resembles a looping, disorienting roller coaster. Accepting this truth is not fatalism—it is the beginning of resilience.

It is too early to forecast Nepal’s political future. But if the RSP fails to bring substantial change in governance, another youth uprising like the September 2025 Gen Z protests is likely. In that scenario, all variants of communist gangs would be washed away in the plural landscape; the RSP would survive but be squeezed to a few dozen seats; the Nepali Congress would gain; and the next election would be hijacked by new political forces with a comfortable new majority.

The central thesis is that Nepal’s 2025–26 political rupture is meaningful only if it produces a genuine change in political consciousness, not merely a change in political personnel—as some critics characterize the present regime, using terms such as “hooligans,” “thuggocrats,” or, in Nepali, “लफङ्गा तन्त्र.”

title: Nepal appeals for collective action against climate risks - risingnepaldaily.com
description: Nepal appeals for collective action against climate risks  risingnepaldaily.com
publisher.title: risingnepaldaily.com
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter,Kathmandu, Sept. 27: Nepal has organised a special event titled ‘Sagarmatha to the Sea’ in New York, United States, to highlight the issue of climate change on the global stage.

Led by Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Nepal hosted the high-level climate-focused special event, ‘Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future’, at the United Nations Headquarters. Nepal had decided to organise the high-level event following the devastating floods in the Bhotekoshi River. A short video of the Bhotekoshi floods was also screened at the event. The event was co-hosted by Bhutan, Maldives, New Zealand, Samoa and Tajikistan, as well the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP).

Addressing the programme, Foreign Minister Khanal stressed the need to address shared climate risks from the mountains to the sea in an integrated manner, noting that the climate system does not recognise political boundaries. "Sagarmatha to the Sea begins with a simple proposition: the climate system does not recognize the boundaries through which we organize our politics," he said.

He said that mountains, rivers, oceans, coastal areas and island regions constitute interconnected ecosystems in terms of climate change, requiring collective and coordinated efforts to address the climate crisis.

The Himalayan region called the - third pole contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside of the polar regions, featuring an inventory of over 63,700 glaciers. Standing at the foot of Himalayas, in 2023, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres described these glaciers as 'icy reservoirs'.

"From there, water descends through glaciers and rivers, nourishing ecosystems and communities before reaching the sea. But, Nepal has lost close to one-third of its ice in the last three decades," said FM Khanal, while adding that their decline alters river flows and threatens livelihoods downstream, while island and coastal nations confront rising seas, erosion and displacement.

He said that science, policy and investment must recognize the ecological continuum connecting mountains, freshwater systems and oceans. Mountains deserve greater prominence in climate processes, including systematic integration across relevant UNFCCC frameworks.

"Keeping 1.5°C within reach is imperative. Every fraction of a degree matters, requiring accelerated emission reductions and implementation of the transition away from fossil fuels agreed under the UNFCCC process," he added.

The foreign minister also stressed on preparedness with stronger early-warning systems, resilient infrastructure, anticipatory action and scientific cooperation.

Likewise, he said that developing countries need adequate, predictable and accessible climate finance, technology and capacity-building. The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage must be sufficiently capitalized and accessible. He informed that Nepal is doing its part with forests covering around 46 per cent of the territory, expanding clean hydropower and electric mobility, and community-led conservation.

Four-year of accelerated action

Foreign Minister Khanal said the remaining period until 2030 should be used as a period of accelerated action to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Addressing a high-level meeting on the Global Development Initiative (GDI) organised at the sidelines of the UNGA, he said urgent action was needed to translate development commitments into results amid growing financing needs, conflicts, the climate emergency and mounting debt pressures in developing countries. Congratulating China on behalf of Nepal on the fifth anniversary of the GDI, he praised China's continued efforts to translate the initiative, proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping, into practical cooperation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed in a statement.

"In five years, the GDI has expanded across the developing world as a platform for partnerships, resource mobilisation, knowledge sharing and practical cooperation," Minister Khanal said.

According to him, the GDI's priorities in poverty reduction, food security, development finance, green development, industrialisation and the digital economy addressed many of the priorities of the Global South.

Noting that the world had entered the final phase towards the 2030 targets, Minister Khanal said only 36 per cent of accessible SDG targets were progressing either on track or at a moderate pace. He said developing countries faced an annual SDG financing gap of around US$4 trillion, while conflicts, the climate crisis and debt pressures had added to the challenges.

Multilateral action called for pandemic preparedness

Addressing a high-level meeting on ‘Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response’, Foreign Minister Khanal said that multilateralism, equity and solidarity must remain at the centre of global efforts to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemics and public health emergencies.

He said the COVID-19 pandemic had demonstrated that a public health emergency arising in one location could develop into a global crisis. "No nation is safe until every nation is safe," he said.

"The pandemic was not merely a health crisis, it also devastated development gains achieved over decades," he said.

Reform needed in int'l financial architecture

Likewise, speaking at the 50th annual meeting of the Group of 77 and China, FM Khanal called for timely reforms to the international financial architecture to increase the voice and representation of developing countries in global economic governance. He stressed the need to renew unity and collective efforts to strengthen multilateralism and said the voice of the Global South should be raised more effectively.

According to him, the UN-centred, rules-based multilateral system should be further strengthened, while implementation of the SDGs should be accelerated through adequate and accessible financial resources, technology transfer and capacity-building.

"There is a need to reduce existing inequalities through economic and digital transformation," he said.

title: Former Chief Justice Rana detained in Nepal — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Former Chief Justice Rana detained in Nepal — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS

full_article:
In Kathmandu, Nepal, police detained former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana. According to the Kathmandu Post, he was detained on Sunday at his residence in the Maharajgunj area.

Detention in Kathmandu

Rana's detention was confirmed by the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office. A senior police source also confirmed that law enforcement officers detained him at his residence in Maharajgunj. Details of the detention were not immediately available at the time of reporting.

Impeachment and court ruling

Cholendra Shumsher Rana assumed the position of Chief Justice on January 1, 2019. On February 13, 2022, an impeachment motion against him was registered in parliament, after which Rana was suspended from office.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

The motion remained under consideration in parliament for a long time. After the parliamentary session ended, the then secretary-general of the Federal Parliament Secretariat sent a letter declaring the impeachment procedure inactive. This letter was challenged in the Supreme Court.

On September 9, the Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court ruled that the impeachment motion against Rana had become moot and dismissed four petitions in the case. The ruling was issued by a four-judge bench led by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma.

full_article:

title: Opinion | Why Nepal’s latest disaster needs a local name—not just a scientific label - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Why Nepal’s latest disaster needs a local name—not just a scientific label  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Government of Nepal has shown wisdom in establishing a committee to find a proper name for the recent devastating floods in the Lende-Bhotékoshi-Trishuli corridor. This is a most welcome and necessary development. Scientists, journalists, policymakers, and ordinary people are all struggling to decide what to call this extraordinary event, and most of the proposed names are unbearably cumbersome and don’t do it justice.

To this admirable task, I want to add only one plea: Please choose a local name. For the moment, and to open to discussion, I want to propose the word gangbal, and I will explain why.

But first, I want you to understand I am opining on this particular topic. It has been my great good fortune to have worked in Nepal since 1973 and with the Tamang peoples of Nuwakot, Rasuwa and Dhading since 1975. The thoughts I present here are my own, and I encourage you to obtain many opinions as you deliberate on endorsing a new name for this terrible phenomenon.

I believe it is in Nepal’s interest to take the lead in generating a simple name for what is a distinctive cascading rock-ice mountain-failure-triggered debris-filled flash-flood of devastating speed, consistency and proportions. The very fact that it takes so many words to describe it underscores the need to give it a unique name. Giving it a Nepali name will underscore the unique vulnerability of her population to a form of disaster not entirely of her own making.

In addition, I want to suggest that you look for a name among the local people who have historically occupied the place where it originated, in remote upper Rasuwa. They are not the only people affected by this disaster, by any means, but their local environmental knowledge has much to teach us, and their extreme vulnerability and resilience deserve our respect.

There are many natural and often catastrophic events that are known by names coming from traditional local communities where such events first or frequently occurred. A famous example is tsunami , which means something like ‘harbour wave’ in Japanese. There, fishing communities were often among the hardest hit when great earthquake-generated ocean waves flooded their harbours, destroying boats, lives and livelihoods. Haboob are ferocious desert dust storms whose name comes from Arabic. Thus, too, the whole world calls seasonal heavy rains ‘monsoon’ after the term mausam in many South Asian languages, including Nepali. A lahar is a destructive lava-mud flow, from Indonesian/Javanese. And perhaps most poignant of all, we still use the Taino word for their storm/wind divinity, ‘hurricane’, although the Taino people, their communities, and their culture, which used to dominate the Caribbean, were devastated almost into extinction by Spanish colonialism.

I encourage the Nepali officials to work closely with the local people of Rasuwa, and with scholars of Tamang language and culture, to find out what they call events like the cataclysm of August 26. In my conversations and research, the word gangbal has come up several times, but others may be able to identify a local word that is better. Gangbal , however, is the most appropriate one I've found so far, with roots in local environmental understanding, as well as being mythically evocative of disasters of legendary proportions and with lessons about how to live safely near rivers capable of such violence.

A long-time friend, host, co-researcher, and colleague, Suryaman Nghyéma Karma Himdung Tamang, from the heavily impacted Ward-5 of Kishpang Rural Municipality, said that his father Lal Bir Himdung Tamang, who was an important local political leader beginning in 2017 BS, had learned the word gangbal from Tschong Gongbo Tamang from Gonggang (below Bremtang, near Gatlang and Goljong). Suryaman recalls that the word was related to the idea of a great water serpent that rode the leading edge of major flood waters, rolling down the precipitous canyons like a giant train, with a bright floodlight shining in front.

According to the founding Tamang politician in Rasuwa, Dawa Finzo, in a recent interview with Tikaram Yatri, these gangbal — the serpents and the rock-ice floods they brought with them—were so large that they could not fit under the bridges, so they washed them away. He specifically remembers one such flood in 2018 BS.

Another friend and colleague, Sete Ram Tamang, recalls his grandfather also telling him about the great gangbal who rode terrible floods down the rivers and warning him never to build houses near the rivers because of the gangbal floods.

Linguist Ajitman Tamang links the idea of gangbal to the myth about the primordial lake in the Kathmandu Valley. According to legend, when Manjushree’s mighty sword cleaved what is today Chobhar Gorge, not only did the waters rush out (in what must have been a catastrophic flood well into what today is India) but it also loosed the great ngyémbu water serpent. Even today, when Tamang people refer to the Kathmandu Valley, they call it Yembu , in honour of this great being and his watery release.

title: Who Will Pay For Nepal’s Climate Cost? - risingnepaldaily.com
description: Who Will Pay For Nepal’s Climate Cost?  risingnepaldaily.com
publisher.title: risingnepaldaily.com
full_article:
post-disaster trauma can be more unsettling than others. It takes away the peace of mind of survivors; it destroys their social network; it leaves them homeless and hopeless. The days and weeks after the disaster are among the worst moments for those who experience it, who suffer its consequences, as well as those who watch from a distance.

Anything that comes as an antidote to these emotions—some comforting words, some assurances (even remote), some gestures, some hugs—can feel like a solace. It may be possible to forget if its cause is attributed to natural forces; it’s harder to accept when human activities are understood to have contributed, particularly when those activities are said to be carried out by people from another geographical location.

As Nepal is struggling to come to terms with the horrendous August 26 tragedy, the rock-and-ice avalanche and subsequent floods that killed hundreds and have traumatised the whole nation, climate justice and loss-and-damage finance have become rallying cries. The argument is straightforward: Nepal has contributed very little to global greenhouse-gas emissions, but it is highly vulnerable to their consequences. Those who have contributed disproportionately to the problem, therefore, have a responsibility to help vulnerable countries like Nepal cope with the damage.

A World Weather Attribution analysis published on September 17, 2026, which identified human-caused climate change as a likely contributing factor in the avalanche and resulting floods, could help Nepal’s case related to climate-related loss and damage.

Who will pay?

United Nations Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), established in 2022 and operationalised at COP28 in 2023, is a dedicated multilateral fund through which Nepal may receive assistance. The FRLD was established to assist vulnerable countries like Nepal. But honestly, there is not much money in this fund. According to the July 2026 FRLD report, the total amount of pledges for the Fund was USD 826.41 million, but the amount received was USD 455.96 million. But the number of funding requests (198), the countries making requests (119), and the amount requested (USD 2.8 billion) are way too high. This gap between the resources available and the demand illustrates the central problem confronting the Fund. Where, then, will the money come from?

Give it whatever name you like—climate finance, loss-and-damage finance, climate compensation or, in the broader political debate, reparations—unless wealthy and high-emitting countries contribute substantially more to the FRLD purse, the gap will get only wider. At the same time, while we point to the Global North and other high-emitting countries for creating climate threats, we should not forget that their economies for a long time depended on carbon-emitting engines.

For example, the prosperity achieved by today's industrialised economies was heavily dependent on fossil fuels: Coal-powered steam engines and locomotives, fossil-fuel-based industries, iron and steel production, mechanisation, fertiliser production, refrigeration, transport, aviation, and so on. Today, climate-related disasters are increasingly affecting developed countries like the US as well. The devastating wildfires in France and Spain in 2026, for example, are also attributed to human-caused warming.

Beyond money

The support and solidarity extended by the global leaders, governments and international organisations after the August 26 tragedy demonstrate their goodwill. Nepal will have to utilise the days to come to gather support from international climate-finance architecture, bilateral and multilateral donors, friendly countries and, most importantly, the FRLD. How we present our case and how we are understood matters a lot. A financial contribution may help a country rescue victims, provide temporary shelter, restore infrastructure and begin reconstruction, but it cannot, by itself, make the climate system safer. Thus, the long-term solution is not rich countries paying the poor countries or poor countries holding rich countries responsible for their past actions.

The long-term solution must therefore involve making the Earth safer and societies more resilient. That requires money, but more than that it requires political will, institutional commitment and empathy—the recognition that what happened in Nepal can happen elsewhere, in different forms and with different consequences—from the global actors. Nepal should tell its own story of loss and damage. We need to make the August 26 tragedy part of the global conversation on climate change.

Will the world listen to Nepal? Maybe they won’t now. But the history of climate diplomacy shows that persistence and perseverance can be rewarding. Vanuatu, a tiny island nation, offers an important lesson. In 1991, Vanuatu, on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, proposed an international insurance mechanism to address the consequences of sea-level rise. The proposal called for contributions from developed countries and envisaged financial support for vulnerable small island and low-lying developing countries suffering loss and damage.

The proposal was not accepted. Yet the idea did not disappear. Small island states and other vulnerable developing countries continued to press the issue through successive rounds of climate negotiations. Vanuatu kept pushing for it and in 2023, the Fund was operationalised.

Nepal's challenge is different from Vanuatu's, but the lesson is relevant. If Nepal can make the world understand not only the magnitude of its losses but also the growing threat that human-caused climate change poses to Himalayan ecosystems, its voice can become part of the larger movement. The question is not simply who will pay Nepal. It is whether the world can collectively build a system capable of helping countries like Nepal survive a crisis they contributed so little to creating.

(The author is a journalist and educator based in Kathmandu.)

title: Opinion | How Nepali literature should respond to political changes - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | How Nepali literature should respond to political changes  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Change is the dominant metaphor in Nepal today. Everything is judged through the lens of change. Political transformation is the most gripping. The shifts marked by the Gen Z protests of 8–9 September 2025 and the subsequent events have become a metonymy of change, and they also constitute the ethos of the times. Political and social changes make up history. Lyrical, poetic or literary manifestations of change are yet to appear. How this is represented in creative literature in Nepal is a subject of study.

In Nepal, change is often attributed to political transformation. Institutional and social transformations occur when a society begins to see new modes of metamorphosis. At such times, political changes are common, especially in countries that must cope with both human and natural interventions. Actions of those who handle state affairs and try to bring things to order after chaotic moments are featured prominently in all discussions in society through media and academia.

With my experience in creative writing, literary criticism, teaching and interpreting literature, I can say that literature is a powerful medium that can represent the moods of changing times more powerfully and successfully than perhaps any other medium of expression. Though it would be too hasty to draw conclusions based on changes I consider important, I would like to say that the consonance between the times and the moods of widespread change is a very important subject. Change is both universal and local. Literature is the most eloquent medium to show both.

Literary response to changing political times does not happen overtly. It often occurs through metaphor, metonymy and symbolism. But there is also another side. Literature can respond directly by promoting writings that are close to propaganda of certain political systems. Literature is both flexible and complex in giving voice to changing political times. This subject has engaged creative writers, literary critics and pedagogues who interpret the nuances of literary writings to show the moods of the times; political change is one of them.

Nepali literature has responded to various changing political times. I would like to recall a couple of interventions in Nepali literature and in political times. King Mahendra’s dissolution of the elected parliament in 1960 and the introduction of what was called a party-less Panchayat system in 1962 marked an important phase of modern Nepali politics and the literary response. Nepali literary writers responded to this political change by writing poetry that did not obtrusively oppose the king’s idea of creating a dream-laden political system, which was the king’s Panchayat vision developed to counter and suppress the multiparty democratic norms.

In an article titled “Literary Response to Panchayat Utopia”, published in the first issue of Martin Chautariʼs journal Studies in Nepali History and Society (June 1996), I made it a point to write that the literary writers responded to the king’s political system by means of rebellious poetic writing that was modernist in style and norm. We followed a method of interpreting history through literature, as propounded by scholar and academic Hayden White in his book Metahistory .

One important characteristic of Nepali democracy is the passionate response of the masses towards it. The literary response is founded on the same passion. We should see where we are at this time. It is a somewhat complex subject that defies any neat analysis, especially at this moment. We can see that the current Nepali literary writings do not overtly reflect the complex and somewhat chaotic character of the political times. Nepali literary writers do not follow the same modus operandi as other analysts.

The Nepali literary practice shows that Nepali writers have their own modes and methods of writing about society and epochal changes. There also exists a tradition of Nepali authors writing in a direct style about the political conditions and the social and ideological changes in the country. Some writers oriented to political ideas see themselves as ‘progressive’ because they believe that the role of the writer is to write with politics as their principal guide. There are others who write on other diverse themes. They do not necessarily draw their motifs from any defined areas. Free choice of themes, styles of expression, and experimentation guide them. But what is also obvious is that such writers saw a dichotomy between their different pursuits, especially in politics and literary writing.

The famous binary of politics and literature has been a subject of discussion among writers and critics. Some say their writing is a non-political praxis. They cite the famous confession of BP Koirala that he is a socialist in politics and an anarchist in literature.

Nepali literature in the current political climate has been neither vocal nor allusive about the political changes. This is a subject of detailed critical study. Literary activities do not evince direct euphoria or dismay about the political changes that have occurred in Nepal. A look at the published works in poetry, fiction and drama shows that the usual trend of writing has not changed. Instead, some interesting and good works written by writers in Nepal and the diaspora about dynastic Nepali history are produced and read.

title: After the deluge - nepalitimes.com
description: After the deluge  nepalitimes.com
publisher.title: nepalitimes.com
full_article:
The catastrophic flood of 26 August put Nepal’s dependence on hydropower under scrutiny, with some suggesting a fundamental rethink. There should certainly be an evaluation, but the disaster is unlikely to bring hydropower development to a halt.

Construction will continue but at a slower pace and under a more demanding technical, regulatory, and financial conditions.

Hydroelectricity has become too important a part of Nepal’s economy to simply stop. Some 260 hydropower projects are currently under construction, and another 360 are in various stages of feasibility assessment, design, financing, or licensing.

Tens of thousands of Nepalis depend on the sector. Cement and steel factories, steel pipe and gate fabricators, suppliers, engineering firms, transporters, consultancies, environmental specialists, insurance companies, banks, and retirement funds all have a stake in the continued construction of hydropower projects.

A sudden halt would have economic consequences extending far beyond the power sector itself.

Nepal has spent the past 25 years building a domestic base of hydropower expertise with engineers, hydrologists, geologists, project developers, environmental specialists, tunneling experts, and construction contractors capable of adapting designs to emerging risks.

Nepali engineers are not starting from scratch. They have long been required to account for hazards such as GLOFs and landslide dammed flash floods. The latest disaster has introduced a third even more deadly category of extreme mountain hazard: floods caused by the collapse of glaciated slopes.

Better data, more rigorous studies and risk assessment, increased monitoring and reliable early warning, safer siting criteria for intake structures and power plants, improved planning for emergencies, and stronger protective infrastructure can reduce risk from all these threats.

These changes will increase costs and development timelines, but the most attractive projects will proceed. Expanded climate-risk assessment, hydro-meteorological modeling, more stringent engineering standards, and rising insurance premiums will all raise investment costs.

Many marginal projects in the pipeline may no longer prove financially viable. Yet, Nepal still possesses an enormous portfolio of attractive hydropower sites. Projects with strong resource characteristics, ready access, manageable risks, and favourable economics will continue to attract developers and financiers.

The hydropower sector has expanded at extraordinary speed over the past decade, with annual additions often exceeding 20% of installed generation capacity.

Nepal enjoys an electricity surplus during much of the year, creating space for regulators, developers, and policymakers to take stock and implement reforms without facing the immediate pressure of energy scarcity.

Hydro and solar projects have spread across 54 districts, not centralised sources. If a majority of this generation capacity was along a single river valley, a flood of this magnitude would have collapsed the entire power infrastructure with few prospects of recovery.

Nepal can build on this proven strategy based on risk mitigation through decentralisation, increased diversification, and allocating risk mitigation responsibilities to the government, project developers, and financing institutions in specific areas where they are most capable of managing those risks.

Nepal’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) currently commits to 15% of electricity generation from non-hydropower renewables by 2035. This target now needs to be reconsidered.

There is solar and wind energy potential, particularly in trans-Himalayan districts with high solar irradiation, low cloud cover, good wind energy, and relatively low exposure to flooding hazards that affect the south of the Himalaya.

Solar and wind generation costs have declined dramatically worldwide and could compete with hydropower in Nepal if the government invests in road and transmission line access to attractive sites in the relatively remote districts like Mustang and Dolpo where resources are most plentiful and land for siting projects is relatively inexpensive.

A higher target, of a quarter to a third of power being generated by non-hydropower sources by 2035, would improve energy security by reducing the country’s exposure to climate-related hydrological risks.

A distinction must be made here between projects that depend on glacier-supported rivers, and those exposed to glacier-related hazards. Most hydropower projects in Nepal larger than 10MW benefit to some degree from glacier and snowmelt contribution to river flows.

A subset of these has significant glacier-hazard exposure in projects located in basins containing large glacierised catchments, unstable glacial lakes or hanging glaciers.

The Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation must therefore identify and map river basins for glacier-hazard exposure. Such information should be made publicly available and pro-actively utilised in basin-level planning and hydropower licensing.

Investors should not have to independently reconstruct hazard assessments that government agencies are better positioned to undertake, and are uniquely positioned to utilise as part of their responsibility to regulate the sector.

100-YEAR FLOODS

Developers have to design and build more secure projects. The era of relying on historical flood records has ended. If so-called ‘100-year floods’ are now occurring every decade, hydrological models and infrastructure design must reflect that reality.

Each project must carry out its own Climate Risk Assessment along the drainage basin before the project is approved. They will need to account for increased frequency of extreme rainfall events as well as those of GLOFs, landslide-dam failures, and glacier-collapse floods.

As the tragic and seemingly futile attempts at rescuing worker trapped in tunnels of Upper Trishuli 3-A (pictured, left), 3-B and Rasuwagadi show, every hydropower project must be required to have Emergency Action Plans by regulation, particularly covering the period during construction when there can be hundreds of workers on site, but also during operations.

Conservative assumptions and proactive safety measures will increasingly become a commercial necessity rather than simply a regulatory compliance issue.

Banks and insurers are likely to demand it. Projects that can demonstrate robust risk assessments and resilient designs should be rewarded by them with lower financing and insurance costs. Those that cannot do so may face significantly higher premiums, regardless of their location.

Engineering adaptations will also become more common. Future powerhouses may need to be located farther above river level, accepting some loss in hydraulic head and power generation capacity in return for safety from flooding.

Critical electrical equipment and substations may need additional protection. Projects facing elevated hazard exposure may require gates capable of isolating headrace and tailrace tunnels during extreme events, preventing floodwater and debris from inundating critical infrastructure. Early warning systems, remote monitoring technologies, and emergency shutdown procedures are also likely to become standard practice.

None of these measures will eliminate risk entirely. Nepal is, located in one of the world’s most dynamic geological and climatic environments. But they can substantially reduce vulnerability.The lesson from the 26 August tragedy is not that hydropower development should stop. It must evolve.

title: Heavy rains cause floods and landslides in Nepal — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Heavy rains cause floods and landslides in Nepal — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Prolonged heavy rains in Nepal have caused floods and landslides in several regions of the country. In the city of Butwal, flooding on the Tinau River swept away six houses along the bank on Saturday evening, while about 1,000 people were evacuated due to rising water levels in the river and nearby streams, Kathmandu Post reports.

The Tinau exceeded its danger level at around 8 p.m. on Saturday. About 200 riverside homes in Butwal are at risk. Authorities initially moved around 500 residents of the Majhuwa area to a temporary site at the Durga temple and later relocated them to safer locations, including schools in Butwal.

Rivers exceeded danger levels

In Chitwan district, the Narayani River and the Riu stream exceeded danger levels due to the rains. At the Devghat hydrological station, the Narayani reached 9.23 metres, while its danger level is 9 metres. The Riu stood at 3.92 metres, compared with its danger level of 3.8 metres.

Flooding also affected the districts of Nawalparasi West and Saptari. In the Susta rural municipality, 172 families were relocated on Friday and Saturday after the Narayani entered settlements. In Saptari, 200 families from Hanumannagar Kankalini municipality and 17 families from Tilathi Koiladi rural municipality were moved to safe locations. In total, water flooded 389 houses in these two districts.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

In Susta's fifth ward, up to 271 homes and animal shelters were flooded, with water reaching about 90 centimetres in some residences. In Saptari, flooding inundated 217 houses: 17 in Tilathi Koiladi and 200 in Hanumannagar Kankalini.

Landslides blocked roads

Landslides and mudslides disrupted traffic on roads in Chitwan, including the Narayanghat–Muglin route. Roads were completely blocked in several places, while traffic was reduced to one lane on some sections. Police said that the connection between Narayanghat and Pokhara could be restored in about two hours if no new obstacles emerge and debris clearing continues uninterrupted.

The risk of floods and landslides also persists in the Karnali region, where water levels in several rivers continued to rise. Landslides blocked the Nagma–Gamgadhi road in Mugu district, the Karnali Highway in Kalikot, and sections of the Karnali transport corridor in Humla district. Local authorities urged residents of areas prone to flooding and landslides to monitor the situation and move to safe locations if necessary.
